name: Control
first: A view that the user changes or taps, such as a button, a toggle, a picker, or a slider, which reports each change through a binding or by calling a closure.

dependsOn.why: A control that changes a value is given a binding to it, and writes the new value through the binding.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The value `$reminders` is a binding to the state `reminders`, as `$nights` is a binding to `nights` on the page of Binding.

what.is: A control is a view that the user changes or taps, such as a button, a toggle, a picker, a slider, or a menu. A control that changes a value, such as a `Toggle`, is given a binding to the value, and writes each new value through it. A `Button` is given a closure, which it calls each time the user taps it.
what.afterExample: The toggle shows whether reminders are on, and writes the new value to `reminders` when the user flips it. No one taps anything here, so line 8 changes the value, as the toggle would, and the `body` runs again. No one taps Save, so its closure never runs.
what.problem: Every app takes input: a setting turned on, a choice from a list, a number of nights, a tap on Save. Controls are views that SwiftUI draws in the style of each platform, and each one gives the code what the user did.
what.how: Apple's documentation says that a toggle is made with a binding and a label, and a button with an action and a label. A control that changes a value reads the value through its binding to draw itself, and writes the new value through the binding when the user changes it. The value is usually state, so the `body` that read it runs again.

when.text: Use SwiftUI's controls for input: a `Toggle` for on or off, a `Button` for an action, and a picker, a slider, or a stepper for a choice or a number.
Don't make a control from a text that reacts to taps. A `Button` already has the platform's look, and VoiceOver reads it as a button.

parts.name: The labels, lines 7 and 9
parts.text: A control's first argument is its label, which says what it does: Reminders for the toggle, and Save for the button. The label can also be any view.

parts.name: The binding, line 7
parts.text: The argument `isOn` gives the toggle a binding to `reminders`. The toggle draws itself on or off from the value, and writes the opposite value when the user flips it.

parts.name: The action, line 9
parts.text: The closure after `Button("Save")` is the button's action. The button keeps no value: it calls this closure each time the user taps it.

steps.text: Line 12 makes a `Settings` and draws it. The state `reminders` starts true.
The `body` runs, and line 6 prints {{reminders: true}}. The toggle reads the value through its binding, and is drawn on.
The toggle appears, and line 8 flips `reminders` to false, as the toggle does through its binding when the user taps it.
The `body` read `reminders`, so it runs again, and line 6 prints {{reminders: false}}. The toggle is now drawn off.
No one taps the button on line 9, so its closure never runs, and the program never prints saved.

end.text: The toggle read and wrote `reminders` through its binding, so the change ran the `body` again. The button would only call its closure when tapped.
